title: DiGraph Structure: Finset-Based Directed Graphs with No Self-Loops
content: `DiGraph V` is a simple structure: a `Finset (V×V)` of directed edges plus a proof of `noSelfLoops`. This minimalist encoding lets Lean's `Finset` machinery handle all cardinality arguments automatically. `outDegree G v` and `inDegree G v` are defined by `Finset.filter` on the first or second component — this makes the handshaking proof a clean algebraic manipulation. `IsBalanced` and `IsEulerianBalanced` are the core predicates: a vertex is balanced iff in-degree = out-degree, and a graph is Eulerian-balanced iff all vertices are balanced.
mathContext: $\text{DiGraph}(V) = (E \subseteq V \times V, \text{no self-loops})$. $\text{outDeg}(v) = |\{e \in E : e.1 = v\}|$, $\text{inDeg}(v) = |\{e \in E : e.2 = v\}|$. $\text{IsBalanced}(v) \iff \text{inDeg}(v) = \text{outDeg}(v)$.
relatedConcepts: Finset.filter: filter a finite set by a predicate
prerequisites: Finset: finite sets in Mathlib with decidable membership
structure in Lean 4: named fields with invariants
DecidableEq V: required for Finset.filter on vertex type

title: Double-Counting via Finset.sum_comm: The Directed Handshaking Lemma
content: Both handshaking lemmas (`sum_outDegree_eq_edgeCount` and `sum_inDegree_eq_edgeCount`) use the same two-step proof. First, rewrite the filter-card as a sum of indicator functions: `|{e : e.1=v}| = ∑_{e∈E} [e.1=v ? 1 : 0]`. Then swap the summation order with `Finset.sum_comm`: `∑_v ∑_{e∈E} [e.1=v] = ∑_{e∈E} ∑_v [e.1=v] = ∑_{e∈E} 1 = |E|`. The directed handshaking equality ∑ outDeg = ∑ inDeg then follows by transitivity through |E|.
relatedConcepts: Finset.sum_comm: exchange order of double summation
prerequisites: Finset.sum_comm: ∑_a ∑_b f(a,b) = ∑_b ∑_a f(a,b) for finite sums
Finset.card_eq_sum_ones: |S| = ∑_{x∈S} 1
Finset.sum_ite_eq': collapses a sum of indicators over a type

title: HasEulerianCircuit: Strengthened with ∃! Coverage for Bijectivity
content: The key design choice for `HasEulerianCircuit` is the use of `∃!` (unique existence) for edge coverage rather than a simple `∃`. The definition requires: (1) walk length = |E|+1, (2) every edge has a *unique* position in the walk (∃!), (3) the walk is closed (head? = getLast?), and (4) every walk step uses a graph edge (hsteps). The uniqueness condition is essential: `ExistsUnique.unique` allows extracting that any two witnesses to the coverage condition must be equal, enabling the bijection-based proof of necessity. Without ∃!, necessity would fail because a multi-use edge could appear at two positions.
mathContext: $\text{HasEulerianCircuit}(G)$: $\exists$ walk of length $|E|+1$, $\forall e \in E,\ \exists! i < |E| : \text{walk}[i]=e.1 \wedge \text{walk}[i+1]=e.2$, and $\text{walk}[0]=\text{walk}[|E|]$ (closed).
relatedConcepts: ExistsUnique.unique: any two witnesses to ∃! are equal
bijection between edges and walk positions
prerequisites: List.get: safe index into a list with an in-bounds proof
ExistsUnique: ∃! x, P x means exactly one x satisfies P
hsteps condition: walk steps must correspond to actual graph edges

title: Circular Shift Bijection: Why Closed Walks Balance Source and Target Counts
content: `closed_walk_balance` proves: for a closed walk (walk[0] = walk[n]), the number of positions where walk[i] = v equals the number where walk[i+1] = v. The proof uses Finset.card_bij with the bijection φ(i) = (i=0 ? n-1 : i-1). At i=0: walk[0]=v implies walk[n]=v (closed walk), so target-position n-1 satisfies walk[n] = v. At i>0: walk[i]=v directly gives target-position i-1. Surjectivity uses the inverse ψ(j) = (j=n-1 ? 0 : j+1). All obligations close with `omega` after `split_ifs`.
mathContext: Closed walk $\implies |\{i < n : w_i = v\}| = |\{i < n : w_{i+1} = v\}|$ for all $v$. Bijection: $\varphi(i) = \begin{cases} n-1 & i=0 \\ i-1 & i > 0 \end{cases}$, inverse $\psi(j) = \begin{cases} 0 & j=n-1 \\ j+1 & j < n-1 \end{cases}$.
relatedConcepts: Finset.card_bij: cardinality equality via explicit bijection
circular shift bijection for closed sequences
split_ifs: case-split on if-then-else in Lean 4
prerequisites: Finset.card_bij: requires maps_to, injectivity, surjectivity proofs
Finset.mem_filter: membership in filter ↔ membership + predicate
closed walk: walk.head? = walk.getLast? encoded as walk[0] = walk[n]

title: Classical.choose + ExistsUnique: Walk Position to Edge Bijections
content: `walk_source_eq_outDegree` proves that |{i < n : walk[i] = v}| = outDeg(v). The bijection maps each edge e ∈ {e∈G.edges : e.1=v} to its unique walk position via `Classical.choose (hcov e he.mem).exists`. Injectivity: if pos(e1) = pos(e2), both endpoints are determined by the walk, so e1 = e2 as pairs. Surjectivity: for position i with walk[i]=v, the edge (walk[i],walk[i+1]) is in G.edges by hsteps, and by `(hcov e he_mem).unique` its canonical position is exactly i. `walk_target_eq_inDegree` is structurally identical, matching on the second endpoint.
mathContext: $|\{i < n : w_i = v\}| = \text{outDeg}(v)$. Bijection: $e \mapsto \text{pos}(e) = \text{Classical.choose}(\exists! \text{ clause for } e)$. Uniqueness: `(hcov e he_mem).unique hspec.1 hi_spec` gives `pos(e) = i` when $i$ also satisfies the coverage condition.
relatedConcepts: Classical.choose: nonconstructive choice from existence proof
ExistsUnique.unique: any two witnesses to ∃! are equal
Prod.ext: two pairs equal iff both components equal
prerequisites: Classical.choose_spec: the chosen element satisfies the property
ExistsUnique.unique: applied as (hcov e hmem).unique to equate walk positions
hsteps: ensures every consecutive walk pair is a graph edge

title: Necessity: Chain inDeg = target-count = source-count = outDeg
content: `eulerian_circuit_implies_balanced` chains four equalities: inDeg(v) = |{i : walk[i+1]=v}| (walk_target_eq_inDegree) = |{i : walk[i]=v}| (closed_walk_balance) = outDeg(v) (walk_source_eq_outDegree). Setup normalizes hcov and hsteps from walk.length-1 to n = G.edges.card, and extracts walk[0]=walk[n] from the head?=getLast? form using List.getLast?_eq_getLast and List.getLast_eq_get. The chain closes with `omega` in three lines.
mathContext: $\text{inDeg}(v) \stackrel{\text{bij}}{=} |\{i < n : w_{i+1}=v\}| \stackrel{\text{closed}}{=} |\{i < n : w_i=v\}| \stackrel{\text{bij}}{=} \text{outDeg}(v)$. Proof: three helper lemmas + omega.
relatedConcepts: necessity direction of Euler's theorem for directed graphs
omega: closes natural number arithmetic goals
prerequisites: closed_walk_balance: rotation bijection equates source and target counts
walk_source_eq_outDegree: source positions biject with outgoing edges
walk_target_eq_inDegree: target positions biject with incoming edges

title: Hierholzer Axioms, Concrete Examples, and Integer Consequences
content: `directed_eulerian_iff` (Hierholzer sufficiency) and `directed_euler_path_iff` (path characterization) are axiomatized — the sufficiency direction requires constructing an Eulerian walk, which demands graph connectivity infrastructure not yet in Mathlib. The concrete examples validate the theory: `directedTriangle` (3-cycle A→B→C→A on Fin 3) is Eulerian-balanced by `native_decide`; `directedPath` (0→1→2) satisfies the Eulerian path degree conditions by `native_decide` and `fin_cases`. The integer consequence `eulerian_balanced_sum_zero` lifts ∑ outDeg = ∑ inDeg to ℤ via `exact_mod_cast`.
mathContext: Hierholzer (1873): balanced + weakly connected → Eulerian circuit exists (axiomatized). Directed path degree conditions: $\text{outDeg}(s) = \text{inDeg}(s)+1$, $\text{inDeg}(t) = \text{outDeg}(t)+1$, all others balanced. Integer form: $\sum_v (\text{outDeg}(v) : \mathbb{Z}) = \sum_v (\text{inDeg}(v) : \mathbb{Z})$ (flow conservation).
relatedConcepts: Hierholzer's algorithm O(|E|) for constructing Eulerian circuits
de Bruijn sequences as Eulerian circuits in de Bruijn graphs
prerequisites: axiom in Lean 4: introduces a proposition without proof
native_decide: native compilation for decidable propositions on finite types
exact_mod_cast: coercion from ℕ to ℤ arithmetic

title: Open-Walk Counting: Target-Count Excess at the Last Vertex
content: `open_walk_last_target_excess` proves that for a walk ending at $w$ (with $w \neq \text{walk}[0]$), the count of positions where $w$ is a target exceeds the count where $w$ is a source by exactly 1. Proof: isolate position $n-1$ from the target filter (it contributes one extra since $\text{walk}[n]=w$), then build a bijection from the remaining target positions $T \setminus \{n-1\}$ to source positions $S$ via $i \mapsto i+1$. The symmetric lemma `open_walk_first_source_excess` handles the first vertex. Together these prove that an open walk creates an asymmetry of exactly ±1 at its endpoints — the counting foundation for the Eulerian path degree conditions.
mathContext: Open walk $v_0 \to \cdots \to v_n$ with $v_0 \neq v_n = w$: $|\{i < n : v_{i+1} = w\}| = |\{i < n : v_i = w\}| + 1$. Bijection: $T \setminus \{n-1\} \to S$ via $i \mapsto i+1$, where $n-1 \in T$ is the extra target position. Surjection inverse: $j \mapsto j-1$ (valid since $v_0 \neq w$ implies $j \geq 1$ for any $j \in S$).
prerequisites: Finset.mem_filter
List.get with bounded index proofs
Finset.card_bij: requires maps_to, injective, surjective proofs

title: maxTrail + maxTrail_closed: Greedy Trail is Closed in Balanced Graphs
content: `maxTrail E v` is a noncomputable greedy function: at each step, if there is an outgoing edge from the current vertex, follow it (removing it from E); otherwise stop. Termination is by `|E|.card` since each step erases one edge. `maxTrail_closed` proves the key theorem: in a balanced digraph, the greedy trail always returns to its starting vertex. The proof is by contradiction: assume the trail ends at `last_v ≠ v`. By maximality (`maxTrailRem_last_no_out`), all outgoing edges of `last_v` were used, so `src_count(last_v) = outDeg(last_v)`. By `open_walk_last_target_excess`: `tgt_count(last_v) = src_count(last_v) + 1`. But `tgt_count ≤ inDeg(last_v) = outDeg(last_v)` (balance). Contradiction: `outDeg + 1 ≤ outDeg`.
mathContext: maxTrail terminates: $|E| \to |E|-1$ per step (erase one edge). maxTrail_closed: if last vertex $u \neq v$, then $\text{outDeg}(u) = \text{src\_count}(u)$ (all outgoing edges used) and $\text{tgt\_count}(u) = \text{src\_count}(u)+1$ (open-walk counting). But $\text{tgt\_count}(u) \leq \text{inDeg}(u) = \text{outDeg}(u)$. So $\text{outDeg}(u)+1 \leq \text{outDeg}(u)$ — contradiction.
prerequisites: Classical.choose: nonconstructive selection of outgoing edge
Finset.card_erase_lt_of_mem: |E\ {e}| < |E|
open_walk_last_target_excess: counting imbalance at last vertex
IsEulerianBalanced: inDeg = outDeg at every vertex

title: Circuit Existence, Balance Preservation, and Path Necessity
content: `circuit_exists` applies `maxTrail_closed` directly: start from any vertex with an outgoing edge, run the greedy trail, which is closed by balance, giving a `DirectedCircuit` structure. `remove_circuit_balanced` (sorry'd) would prove that removing a circuit's edges preserves balance — the circuit passes through each vertex equally often as source and target (by `closed_walk_balance`), so both degrees decrease by the same amount. `euler_path_implies_degree_balance` (fully proved) establishes necessity for Eulerian paths: in an open walk from $s$ to $t$, applying `open_walk_first_source_excess` to $s$ and `open_walk_last_target_excess` to $t$ yields the asymmetric degree conditions; closed-walk balance handles interior vertices. The single remaining sorry (`remove_circuit_balanced`) is the last obstacle to eliminating the `directed_eulerian_iff` axiom.
mathContext: Circuit existence: $G$ balanced, $|E| \geq 1 \Rightarrow \exists$ directed circuit in $G$. Remove circuit: for each $v$, circuit passes through $v$ equally as source ($s_v$ times) and target ($t_v = s_v$ times by closed-walk balance), so $\text{outDeg}_{G'}(v) = \text{outDeg}_G(v) - s_v = \text{inDeg}_G(v) - s_v = \text{inDeg}_{G'}(v)$. Path necessity: $s$ has $\text{outDeg}(s) = \text{inDeg}(s)+1$ (extra source at start); $t$ has $\text{inDeg}(t) = \text{outDeg}(t)+1$ (extra target at end).
prerequisites: maxTrail_closed: greedy trail is closed in balanced graph
DirectedCircuit: structure with head_eq_last, length_ge_2, steps_in_G
DiGraph.removeEdgeSet: G' = G minus edge set S
Finset.sdiff: set difference for Finset

title: Trail-Support Trilogy: Exhaustion, Step-Membership, Step-Distinctness by Strong Induction on |E|
content:
Three private lemmas form the bridge between maxTrail's recursive definition and its use in the balance-contradiction proof. All three share the same induction skeleton: `Nat.strong_rec_on` on `E.card`, case-split on whether `(E.filter (fun e => e.1 = v)).Nonempty`, and in the recursive case unfold `maxTrail E v = v :: maxTrail (E.erase c) c.2` where `c = hout.choose`.

**maxTrail_last_exhausted** (734–792): every outgoing edge of the trail's last vertex was consumed. Strong-induction lets the inner trail `maxTrail (E.erase c) c.2` share the same last vertex as the outer trail (`List.getLast_cons`), so the IH applied at `E.erase c` directly handles edges other than `c`; the case `e = c` uses step 0 of the outer trail (the edge `c` itself).

**maxTrail_steps_in_E** (794–829): every consecutive walk-pair is an actual graph edge. Step 0 is `(v, c.2)` which equals `c ∈ E` (using `hinner_start : maxTrail (E.erase c) c.2)[0] = c.2`); step `i+1` reduces to the inner-trail IH and lifts back to `E` via `Finset.mem_of_mem_erase`.

**maxTrail_steps_distinct** (831–915): no edge appears at two positions. Four-way case analysis on `i, j ∈ {0, succ}`: cases `(0, 0)` and `(succ, succ)` are immediate / inner-IH; the two mixed cases use the fact that step 0 produces edge `c` while any step `j' + 1` produces an edge in `E.erase c`, and `Finset.not_mem_erase c E` rules out the collision. This distinctness is exactly what `Finset.card_bij` needs for the injection from outgoing edges to source-positions of the last vertex in STEP B of maxTrail_closed.
mathContext:
Three claims about $	ext{maxTrail}(E, v)$ proved by strong induction on $|E|$: (1) **exhaustion**: $ orall e \in E,\ e.1 = 	ext{last\_v} \Rightarrow \exists i,\ 	ext{step}(i) = e$; (2) **step-membership**: $ orall i,\ 	ext{step}(i) \in E$; (3) **distinctness**: $i 
eq j \Rightarrow 	ext{step}(i) 
eq 	ext{step}(j)$. Inductive structure: write $	ext{maxTrail}(E, v) = v :: 	ext{maxTrail}(E \setminus \{c\}, c.2)$ where $c$ is the chosen outgoing edge. The IH at $E \setminus \{c\}$ (with cardinality $|E| - 1$) handles all inner-trail steps; the base step (step 0) is identified with $c$ via $	ext{hinner\_start}$ and Prod.mk.inj. Distinctness across step 0 / step $j+1$ uses $c 
otin E \setminus \{c\}$.
relatedConcepts: Nat.strong_rec_on: strong induction over natural numbers
List.getLast_cons: last of (v :: t) equals last of t when t ≠ []
Classical.choose / Finset.Nonempty.choose pattern for selecting an outgoing edge
prerequisites: maxTrail recursive definition: greedy edge-consumption with Finset.erase
maxTrail_head' and maxTrail_nonempty': trail starts at v, is non-empty
Prod.mk.inj_iff: ordered-pair equality componentwise
Finset.Nonempty.choose / choose_spec: select witness from nonempty Finset

title: maxTrail_closed: Five-Step Balance-Contradiction Proof
content: The proof of `maxTrail_closed` is the structural core of Hierholzer's theorem. It is organized into five labelled STEPs (A-E) that compose into a balance contradiction. **STEP A** (`maxTrail_last_exhausted`): every outgoing edge of `last_v` in $G$ appears as some position of the trail, established as a `∀ e ∈ G.edges, e.1 = last_v → ∃ i ...` lemma. **STEP B** (`h_src_eq_out`): bijection between outgoing edges and source positions of `last_v`, proved via `Finset.card_bij` with `Classical.choose` selecting the unique trail position for each edge; surjectivity uses `maxTrail_steps_distinct` to rule out duplicate edges. **STEP C** (`h_tgt_le_in`): target positions of `last_v` inject into incoming edges via the position-to-edge map; uses `Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn`. **STEP D** (`h_count`): applies `open_walk_last_target_excess` to extract `tgt_count = src_count + 1`. **STEP E** (`hbal_last`): substitution of `inDeg = outDeg` followed by `omega` closes the contradiction `outDeg + 1 ≤ outDeg`. The trivial closed case (trail length ≤ 1) is handled by `interval_cases` + `maxTrail_head'` at the top.
mathContext: Proof by contradiction. Assume $\text{last\_v} \neq v$. Then: $\text{outDeg}(\text{last\_v}) \stackrel{A,B}{=} \text{src\_count} \stackrel{D}{=} \text{tgt\_count} - 1 \stackrel{C}{\leq} \text{inDeg}(\text{last\_v}) - 1 \stackrel{\text{bal}}{=} \text{outDeg}(\text{last\_v}) - 1$ — contradiction. The five-step decomposition is what makes the proof modular: each step uses one independent lemma from the infrastructure section, so the dependencies form a directed acyclic graph rather than a single monolithic argument.
prerequisites: maxTrail_last_exhausted: every outgoing edge of the last vertex is consumed
maxTrail_steps_distinct: no edge appears at two positions in the maximal trail
open_walk_last_target_excess: open-walk counting imbalance
IsEulerianBalanced: in-degree = out-degree at every vertex

title: DirectedCircuit Structure and circuit_exists
content: `DirectedCircuit G` packages four fields: `walk : List V` (the vertex sequence), `head_eq_last` (closure), `length_ge_2` (non-triviality), and `steps_in_G` (every consecutive pair is a graph edge). This is the minimum data required to state Hierholzer's splicing operation downstream. `circuit_exists` then converts `maxTrail_closed` into a `Nonempty (DirectedCircuit G)`: pick any edge $e_0 \in G$, start the trail at $v = e_0.1$, use `maxTrail_closed` for closure, and use the presence of $e_0$ to force trail length ≥ 2. This is the first explicit *constructive content* of the file beyond the necessity direction — it builds a concrete circuit from the abstract balance hypothesis.
mathContext: $G$ balanced, $G.\text{edges} \neq \emptyset$ $\Rightarrow$ $\exists$ directed circuit. Construction: pick $e_0 \in G$, start `maxTrail` at $e_0.1$; closure by `maxTrail_closed`, length ≥ 2 because $e_0$ provides one step, and `steps_in_G` follows from `maxTrail_steps_in_E`. The `Nonempty (DirectedCircuit G)` wrapper allows the consumer to extract a witness via `Nonempty.some` or `Classical.choice`.
prerequisites: maxTrail_closed: maximal trail is closed in balanced digraph
Finset.Nonempty.exists witness extraction

title: walkEdges + DiGraph.removeEdgeSet + remove_circuit_balanced (sorry'd)
content: `walkEdges` extracts the edge list of a walk via `List.range (walk.length - 1) |>.filterMap (i ↦ some (walk[i], walk[i+1]))`. `DiGraph.removeEdgeSet` subtracts a `Finset (V×V)` from the edges, with `noSelfLoops` preserved by `Finset.sdiff_subset`. `remove_circuit_balanced` is the **only sorry** in the file: it claims that removing a circuit's edges preserves balance, with proof sketch *circuit_passes_through_each_vertex_same_#times_as_src_and_tgt → inDeg_outDeg_each_decrease_by_same_amount*. The sorry is blocked on the `Finset.sdiff` / `Finset.filter` distributivity API — specifically, an expression of the form $|E \setminus S \cap F| = |E \cap F| - |S \cap F|$ for $S \subseteq E$ — which requires `Finset.card_sdiff` with a `disjoint`-or-`subset`-hypothesis chain that the current Lean Genius infrastructure does not have ready.
mathContext: Removing circuit $C$ from balanced $G$: for each vertex $v$, $C$ passes through $v$ as source $s_v$ times and as target $t_v$ times. By `closed_walk_balance` on $C$ (which is closed), $s_v = t_v$. Then $\text{outDeg}_{G'}(v) = \text{outDeg}_G(v) - s_v = \text{inDeg}_G(v) - t_v = \text{inDeg}_{G'}(v)$. The proof needs an explicit injection from circuit-source positions to outgoing edges of $G$ at $v$, then `Finset.card_sdiff` for the degree decrement.
relatedConcepts: closed_walk_balance: source-count equals target-count in closed walks
Hierholzer splicing: peel circuit, recurse on remainder
prerequisites: Finset.sdiff_subset (used in noSelfLoops preservation)
Finset.card_sdiff (blocked dependency)

title: euler_path_implies_degree_balance: Necessity for Eulerian Paths (Fully Proved)
content:
`euler_path_implies_degree_balance` is the necessity half of `directed_euler_path_iff` (which itself is still axiomatized in this file). For an Eulerian path from $s 	o t$ ($s 
eq t$), it proves three simultaneous claims: $	ext{outDeg}(s) = 	ext{inDeg}(s) + 1$, $	ext{inDeg}(t) = 	ext{outDeg}(t) + 1$, and every other vertex is balanced. The proof normalizes `hcov` and `hsteps` from `walk.length - 1` to `n = G.edges.card`, extracts `walk[0] = s` and `walk[n] = t`, then applies the three open-walk counting lemmas: `open_walk_first_source_excess` (source asymmetry at $s$), `open_walk_last_target_excess` (target asymmetry at $t$), `open_walk_interior_balanced` (interior balance for $v 
eq s, t$). Each is composed with the source/target bijections (`walk_source_eq_outDegree`, `walk_target_eq_inDegree`) to translate position counts into in/out degrees. The case $n = 0$ (empty graph, walk = single vertex) is ruled out by contradiction with $s 
eq t$. This theorem is sorry-free and provides the constructive content needed to eventually eliminate the `directed_euler_path_iff` axiom (paired with a path-existence sufficiency proof).
mathContext: Open walk $s = w_0 \to w_1 \to \cdots \to w_n = t$ with $s \neq t$. Source / target counts: $|\{i < n : w_i = v\}| = \text{outDeg}(v)$, $|\{i < n : w_{i+1} = v\}| = \text{inDeg}(v)$. Then: at $s$: $\text{outDeg}(s) - \text{inDeg}(s) = 1$ (extra source at $w_0$); at $t$: $\text{inDeg}(t) - \text{outDeg}(t) = 1$ (extra target at $w_n$); at interior $v$: $\text{outDeg}(v) = \text{inDeg}(v)$ (no asymmetry).
relatedConcepts: necessity direction of Eulerian path theorem
prerequisites: HasEulerianPath: walk with unique-edge-coverage + open endpoints
open-walk counting trio (first source excess / last target excess / interior balanced)

title: Applications: De Bruijn Sequences, BEST Theorem, Genome Assembly
content:
The directed Eulerian theorem has three celebrated applications that transform abstract degree-balance into practical algorithms.

**De Bruijn sequences** (de Bruijn 1946, Good 1946): A de Bruijn sequence of order n over alphabet Σ is a cyclic sequence in which every n-letter word appears exactly once. Construction: build the de Bruijn graph B(n,Σ) with vertices = (n-1)-grams and edges = n-grams; each vertex has in-degree = out-degree = |Σ|, so the directed Eulerian theorem guarantees an Eulerian circuit, which spells the de Bruijn sequence. For binary sequences of order n, this gives a sequence of length 2ⁿ containing every binary n-bit string exactly once — used in Gray codes, card tricks, and robotic motion planning.

**BEST theorem** (van Aardenne-Ehrenfest, de Bruijn 1951; Smith, Tutte 1941–48): For an Eulerian directed graph, the number of Eulerian circuits starting at vertex $w$ is $t_w(G) \times \prod_{v \neq w} (\text{outDeg}(v)-1)!$, where $t_w(G)$ counts arborescences rooted at $w$ (computable via the Matrix-Tree theorem as a determinant). The formula is the directed analogue of the BEST for undirected graphs and connects Eulerian enumeration to algebraic graph theory.

**Genome assembly** (Pevzner, Tang, Waterman 2001): The EULER assembler fragments a genome into overlapping k-mers, builds the de Bruijn graph (vertices = (k-1)-mers, edges = k-mers), and reconstructs the genome as an Eulerian path. This transformed computational biology: next-generation sequencing assembly became an instance of the directed Eulerian path problem, tractable in O(|E|) via Hierholzer's algorithm.
mathContext: **De Bruijn graph**: $B(n, \Sigma)$ has vertex set $\Sigma^{n-1}$, edge $(w_1\ldots w_{n-1}) \to (w_2\ldots w_n)$ for each $w_n \in \Sigma$. Every vertex: $\text{outDeg} = \text{inDeg} = |\Sigma|$. **BEST**: $\#(\text{Eulerian circuits at }w) = t_w(G) \cdot \prod_v (d^+(v)-1)!$. **Genome assembly**: $k$-mer graph $\to$ Eulerian path $\to$ genome sequence. Handshaking lemma implies balanced iff $\sum_v \text{outDeg}(v) = \sum_v \text{inDeg}(v) = |E|$ (flow conservation).
prerequisites: directed Eulerian theorem (directed_eulerian_iff)
Hierholzer's algorithm O(|E|)
Matrix-Tree theorem for arborescence counting
combinatorics of cyclic sequences
